insider_note: Multiplying top and bottom under the root by (5−x) is the move that turns an awkward ratio of two DIFFERENT linear expressions into a single linear numerator over one quadratic root — after that, this becomes exactly the same A·Dr′+B method used elsewhere in this chapter.

steps.label: Rationalise the square root
lines: A root of one bracket over another is hard to

lines.text: integrate, so multiply above and below by
√(5−x) to put a single root underneath.

steps.why: Multiplying inside the root by (5−x)/(5−x) turns the awkward ratio of two DIFFERENT expressions into a single (5−x) sitting over the square root of their product — now a familiar linear-over-root shape.
common_mistakes: Trying to integrate the original √[(5−x)/(x−2)] form directly without this rationalising step first.
Sign slip expanding (x−2)(5−x) — expand as x(5−x)−2(5−x) = 5x−x²−10+2x, one term at a time.
steps.memory_tip: Multiply by (5−x)/(5−x) under the root to turn a QUOTIENT of two linear terms into a single linear numerator over their product.

steps.label: Write the numerator as A·Dr′ + B and solve for A, B

lines.text: Compare the coefficients on both sides:

steps.why: With the integrand now in the familiar linear-numerator-over-root-of-quadratic shape, the standard A·Dr′+B split applies directly.
common_mistakes: Using the ORIGINAL denominator (x−2)(5−x) instead of its expanded quadratic form 7x−10−x² when differentiating.
steps.memory_tip: 7(1/2)=7/2, and 5−7/2=3/2 — subtract, don't add, when isolating B.

steps.label: Substitute back and split the integral
steps.why: The A-part is again an f′(x)/√f(x) form worth 2√f(x), and here the outside 1/2 exactly cancels that 2, leaving a clean √(7x−10−x²) with no leftover coefficient.
common_mistakes: Missing the factor-of-2 rule for ∫f′/√f dx once again.
Forgetting the leftover B=3/2 multiplier on the second integral.
steps.memory_tip: (1/2)×2=1 — the standard factor of 2 cancels the outside 1/2 exactly, a clean coincidence worth noticing.

steps.label: Complete the square for the final answer

lines.text: Put u = x − 7/2 and a = 3/2, so du = dx

steps.why: The quadratic completes to a bounded (3/2)²−(x−7/2)² form, so the leftover integral is the standard Sin⁻¹ result; clearing the internal halves gives (2x−7)/3 inside it.
common_mistakes: Sign slip completing the square on −x²+7x−10, which needs the leading −1 factored out first.
Leaving the Sin⁻¹ argument un-simplified as (x−7/2)/(3/2) instead of (2x−7)/3.
steps.memory_tip: Factor out the leading −1 BEFORE completing the square whenever the x² coefficient is negative — skipping this is the most common slip on this question.
